title: Portfolio Construction and the No-Trade Region

maps.tested: Rated Very Important by the sheet; no exam recall in this dataset names it directly, though 'portfolio manager numerical' may belong here.
maps.specifics: Alpha refinement and neutralisation, transaction costs, and the optimal no-trade region: the band [-sell cost, +purchase cost] around the target. The four construction techniques (screens, stratification, linear programming, quadratic programming) form a ready-made four-statement audit.

vardeezReading: IM-4: Very Important, with two pointers: "1. Transaction Costs and No-Trade Region 2. Portfolio Construction Techniques".

selectors.name: Alpha refinement: scaling, trimming, neutralisation
selectors.what: Refining raw alphas before optimisation: scale them so that Std{alpha} = volatility x IC (alpha = volatility x IC x score; IC 0.05 and residual risk 30% give 1.5%), trim outliers beyond about three times the scale, and neutralise against benchmark (alpha' = alpha - beta x alpha_B), cash, risk-factor or industry (subtract the cap-weighted industry average alpha) bets.
selectors.theory: Why alphas are refined rather than the optimiser constrained (constraints partly safeguard against poor research), what the scale of alpha should be, why extreme alphas are zeroed or pulled in to three times scale, and what each neutralisation removes (benchmark-neutral gives a beta of 1 and avoids benchmark timing; cash-neutral means no active cash position).

selectors.name: Transaction costs amortised over holding period
selectors.what: Annualised transactions cost = round-trip cost / holding period in years, compared with the annual alpha (USD 0.75 on USD 100 is 3% a year for a 6-month holding and 0.75% a year for a 24-month holding).
selectors.theory: Costs occur at a point in time while alpha accrues over the horizon, so a shorter holding period raises the annual cost; costs turn the one-dimensional risk-aversion trade-off into a two-dimensional one, so the scale of alphas must be precise.

selectors.name: No-trade region: MCVA, alpha and Leland band
selectors.what: The current portfolio is optimal while -SC <= MCVA <= PC, with MCVA = alpha - 2 x lambda_A x psi_P x MCAR; equivalently alpha lies within 2 x lambda_A x psi_P x MCAR - SC and 2 x lambda_A x psi_P x MCAR + PC. Bandwidth = PC + SC (0.50% + 0.75% = 1.25%); net benefit of buying or selling is the distance outside the band (MCVA 0.80% gives 0.30% from buying; MCVA -1.30% gives 0.55% from selling). Leland: around an optimal 60/40 allocation with linear costs, trade back to the boundary of the region, not the target.
selectors.theory: Why a band exists (a trade must recover its cost), why the width is the sum of purchase and sell costs, why alpha must fall by the whole width after a purchase before a sale is considered, and why trading only to the boundary cuts turnover and costs roughly in half with effectively no change in risk; the region's size depends on costs, risk aversion and the expected return and risk of stocks and bonds.

selectors.name: Four techniques: screens, stratification, LP, QP
selectors.what: Four-statement audit of the strengths and weaknesses of the techniques: screens (rank by alpha, robust because they use only ranking, but ignore all other alpha information and control risk fragmentarily), stratification (exclusive categories at benchmark weights), linear programming (non-exclusive risk dimensions, explicit costs and limits, uses all alpha information) and quadratic programming (handles alpha, risk and costs, includes LP as a special case, but needs far more inputs and the optimiser exploits noise in covariances).
